label: prop:oracles
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:oracles}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian}, consider a
nonstationary iterate $x^k$ of Algorithm~\ref{alg:cubic}.
Let the columns of
$Q^k\in\mathbb R^{d\times r_k}$ form a Euclidean orthonormal basis of
$\mathcal S^k$, where $r_k=\dim\mathcal S^k\le3$. Define
\[
 B^k=(Q^k)^T\nabla^2f(x^k)Q^k.
\]
The step is $s^k=Q^k a^k$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reduced-solution}
 a^k=-(B^k+\lambda_k I)^{-1}(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k),
\end{equation}
and $\lambda_k$ is the unique positive solution of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:secular}
 \lambda_k=H\bigl\|(B^k+\lambda_k I)^{-1}
                                  (Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k)\bigr\|.
\end{equation}
It satisfies $\lambda_k\le\sqrt{H\|\nabla f(x^k)\|}$.
After initialization, each iteration needs one new gradient and
at most three HVPs, and no function evaluations.
head: environment
name: Reduced solve and oracle count

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $Q^k$ is orthonormal, substituting $s=Q^k a$ into the model gives
\[
 \nabla f(x^k)^TQ^k a+\tfrac12 a^TB^k a+\tfrac H3\|a\|^3.
\]
Convexity gives $B^k\succeq0$. Since $H>0$, this reduced objective
is strictly convex and coercive, so it has a unique minimizer.
Its first-order condition is
$(B^k+H\|a^k\|I)a^k=-(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k)$.
The projected gradient is nonzero because the full gradient is
nonzero and belongs to $\mathcal S^k$. Thus $a^k\ne0$ and
$\lambda_k=H\|a^k\|>0$.
Also $B^k\succeq0$, so $B^k+\lambda_k I$ is invertible.
This proves \eqref{eq:reduced-solution}--\eqref{eq:secular}.

To verify uniqueness directly, diagonalize $B^k$.
The norm on the right of \eqref{eq:secular} is a strictly decreasing
continuous function of positive $\lambda_k$, with positive
(possibly infinite) limit at zero and limit zero at infinity.
The left side increases strictly from zero to infinity, so there
is exactly one intersection. Since
$\|(B^k+\lambda_k I)^{-1}\|\le1/\lambda_k$, the equation also gives
$\lambda_k^2\le H\|(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k)\|=H\|\nabla f(x^k)\|$.

The directions defining $\mathcal S^k$ are available before the model
solve. One HVP for each column of $Q^k$ determines
$\nabla^2f(x^k)Q^k$ and hence $B^k$. Forming
$(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k)$ uses the current gradient already in memory.
The scalar solve and all reduced linear algebra then use only
these coefficients, with no further objective-oracle calls.
The single new gradient is $\nabla f(x^{k+1})$, used in the
correction and in the next iteration. With the supplied $H$, the
algorithm requires no function-value test.

label: lem:invariance
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Model step and level-set invariance

label: eq:stationarity-along-step
title: Proof
body_md:
Convexity gives $\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0$.  Hence the objective in
\eqref{eq:model} is strictly convex and coercive on $S$, owing to the term
$H\|u\|^3/3$.  It has a unique minimizer, and its first-order condition is
\eqref{eq:model-stationarity}.  Taking the inner product of that condition
with $s\in S$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stationarity-along-step}
 \nabla f(x)^Ts=-s^T\nabla^2f(x)s-H\|s\|^3.
\end{equation}

If $\nabla f(x)=0$, uniqueness gives $s=0$, and all the conclusions are
immediate.  Suppose therefore that $\nabla f(x)\ne0$.  Because
$-\nabla f(x)\in S$ is a strict descent direction for the cubic objective
at zero, its minimizer is nonzero.  Equation
\eqref{eq:stationarity-along-step} then gives
$\nabla f(x)^Ts<0$, so differentiability implies
$f(x+ts)<f(x)\le f(x^0)$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$.

For every $0<t\le1$, substituting
\eqref{eq:stationarity-along-step} into the full cubic expression at $ts$
gives
\begin{align*}
 &t\nabla f(x)^Ts
 +\frac{t^2}{2}s^T\nabla^2f(x)s
 +\frac{Ht^3}{3}\|s\|^3\\
 &\qquad=-t(1-t/2)s^T\nabla^2f(x)s
          -Ht(1-t^2/3)\|s\|^3<0.
\end{align*}
Suppose that the segment from $x$ to $x+s$ leaves $\mathcal C_0$, and set
\[
 t_{\rm exit}=\inf\{t\in[0,1]:f(x+ts)>f(x^0)\}.
\]
The initial strict decrease gives $t_{\rm exit}>0$.  Continuity gives
$f(x+t_{\rm exit}s)=f(x^0)$, and the segment preceding this point is
contained in $\mathcal C_0$.  We may therefore apply
\eqref{eq:taylor-upper} on that segment.  The preceding strict inequality
then yields
\begin{align*}
 f(x+t_{\rm exit}s)
 &\le f(x)+t_{\rm exit}\nabla f(x)^Ts
   +\frac{t_{\rm exit}^2}{2}s^T\nabla^2f(x)s
   +\frac{Ht_{\rm exit}^3}{3}\|s\|^3\\
 &<f(x)\le f(x^0),
\end{align*}
contradicting the definition of $t_{\rm exit}$.  Thus
$[x,x+s]\subseteq\mathcal C_0$.

The Taylor upper bound is now valid for the full step.  Using
\eqref{eq:stationarity-along-step},
\begin{align*}
 f(x+s)-f(x)
 &\le\nabla f(x)^Ts+\tfrac12s^T\nabla^2f(x)s
                      +\tfrac H3\|s\|^3\\
 &=-\tfrac12s^T\nabla^2f(x)s-\tfrac{2H}{3}\|s\|^3.
\end{align*}
Rearranging proves \eqref{eq:two-decreases}.  Its right-hand side is
strictly positive when $s\ne0$.
head: environment

label: lem:defect
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Decrease controls the projected gradient

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance} places the entire step segment in
$\mathcal C_0$, so the gradient Taylor estimate
\eqref{eq:taylor-gradient} applies.  Subtracting
\eqref{eq:model-stationarity} from the projected new gradient gives
\begin{align*}
 \|\Pi_S\nabla f(x+s)\|
 &\le\|\nabla f(x+s)-\nabla f(x)-\nabla^2f(x)s\|
       +H\|s\|^2\\
 &\le2H\|s\|^2.
\end{align*}
The cubic term in \eqref{eq:two-decreases} gives
\[
 \|s\|^3\le\frac{3}{2H}\bigl(f(x)-f(x+s)\bigr).
\]
Taking the power $2/3$ and multiplying by $2H$ proves the second
inequality because
$2H(3/(2H))^{2/3}=(18H)^{1/3}$.
head: environment

label: lem:gradient-decrease
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Gradient decrease

label: eq:decrease-constant
title: Proof
body_md:
For this proof, abbreviate the gradient-decrease coefficient by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decrease-constant}
 \mathcal L:=L_0+\sqrt{2HL_0D_0}.
\end{equation}
The segment from $x^\star$ to $x\in\mathcal C_0$ lies in the convex set
$\mathcal C_0$.  Since $\nabla f(x^\star)=0$, integration of the Hessian
along this segment gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gradient-level-bound}
 \|\nabla f(x)\|\le L_0\|x-x^\star\|\le L_0D_0.
\end{equation}
In particular, applying this bound at $x^0$ shows that
$\nabla f(x^0)\ne0$ implies $L_0D_0>0$, and hence $\mathcal L>0$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance}, the Taylor upper bound applies to the
accepted step.  By the minimizing property in \eqref{eq:model}, its full
cubic expression is no larger than the value at
$-\nabla f(x)/\mathcal L\in S$.  Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 f(x+s)-f(x)
 &\le\nabla f(x)^Ts+\tfrac12s^T\nabla^2f(x)s
                      +\tfrac H3\|s\|^3\\
 &\le-\frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{\mathcal L}
 +\frac{\nabla f(x)^T\nabla^2f(x)\nabla f(x)}{2\mathcal L^2}
 +\frac{H\|\nabla f(x)\|^3}{3\mathcal L^3}\\
 &\le-\frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{\mathcal L}
 \left(1-\frac{L_0}{2\mathcal L}
          -\frac{H\|\nabla f(x)\|}{3\mathcal L^2}\right).
\end{align*}
The last inequality uses
$\|\nabla^2f(x)\|\le L_0$.  Also $L_0/(2\mathcal L)\le1/2$, and
$\mathcal L^2\ge2HL_0D_0\ge2H\|\nabla f(x)\|$ by
\eqref{eq:gradient-level-bound}, so
$H\|\nabla f(x)\|/(3\mathcal L^2)\le1/6$.  The last parenthesis is
therefore at least $1/3$, which gives
\[
 f(x+s)-f(x)\le-\frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{3\mathcal L}.
\]
Rearranging proves \eqref{eq:gradient-budget}.  Only the accepted step
uses a Taylor estimate; the comparison point
$x-\nabla f(x)/\mathcal L$ is used solely to compare explicit cubic
expressions and need not belong to $\mathcal C_0$.
head: environment

label: lem:weights
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weight identities

title: Proof
body_md:
The recurrence is the positive root of
$\omega_{k+1}^2-\omega_{k+1}-\omega_k^2=0$.
The difference identity follows, including $k=0$ under
$\omega_{-1}=0$. Summation proves the cumulative identity.
For $t>0$, the inequalities
$2t\le\sqrt{1+4t^2}<2t+1$ imply that the next weight lies between
$t+1/2$ and $t+1$. Starting from $\omega_0=1$ gives the growth bounds.
head: environment

label: prop:iteration
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Properties of one iteration

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance} inductively, since
$\nabla f(x^k)\in\mathcal S^k$ and $x^0\in\mathcal C_0$.
This proves existence and uniqueness of every model step, invariance,
and monotonicity. Orthogonal projections exist for all subspaces,
including those with redundant or zero directions.
For $k\ge1$, \eqref{eq:orthogonalities} follows from
$h^k=(I-\Pi_{\mathcal V^k})\nabla f(x^k)$; for $k=0$ it follows from
$x^k-x^0=0$ and $z^{-1}=0$.
The gradient estimate is Lemma~\ref{lem:gradient-decrease}.
Finally, $\mathcal V^{k+1}\subseteq\mathcal S^k$, and therefore
\[
 \|e^{k+1}\|=\|\Pi_{\mathcal V^{k+1}}\nabla f(x^{k+1})\|
 \le\|\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\nabla f(x^{k+1})\|.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:defect} now gives \eqref{eq:defect-budget}.
head: environment

label: lem:reserve
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weighted interval estimate

label: eq:weighted-gap-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
The weight identities in Lemma~\ref{lem:weights} give
$\omega_i=\omega_i^2-\omega_{i-1}^2$.  Summation by parts therefore yields
the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-gap-identity}
 \omega_k^2\Delta_{k+1}
 +\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 =\omega_{\ell-1}^2\Delta_\ell+\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i\Delta_i.
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\[
 \sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i\Delta_i
 =\omega_k^2\Delta_k-\omega_{\ell-1}^2\Delta_\ell
   +\sum_{i=\ell}^{k-1}\omega_i^2(\Delta_i-\Delta_{i+1}),
\]
and substituting $\Delta_k=\Delta_{k+1}+d_k$ gives
\eqref{eq:weighted-gap-identity}.

Convexity at $x^i$ and the decomposition
$\nabla f(x^i)=h^i+e^i$ imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta_i
 &\le \nabla f(x^i)^T(x^i-x^\star)\\
 &=(h^i)^T(x^i-x^0)+(h^i)^T(x^0-x^\star)
   +(e^i)^T(x^i-x^\star)\\
 &\le (h^i)^T(x^0-x^\star)+D_0\|e^i\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $(h^i)^T(x^i-x^0)=0$ by \eqref{eq:orthogonalities}, and
$\|x^i-x^\star\|\le D_0$ because $x^i\in\mathcal C_0$.  Since
$z^i-z^{i-1}=\omega_i h^i$, summing the last inequality after multiplication
by $\omega_i$ gives
\[
 \sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i\Delta_i
 \le (x^0-x^\star)^T(z^k-z^{\ell-1})
     +D_0\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i\|e^i\|.
\]

The second orthogonality in \eqref{eq:orthogonalities} gives a Pythagorean
identity at every update:
\[
 \|z^i\|^2
 =\|z^{i-1}+\omega_i h^i\|^2
 =\|z^{i-1}\|^2+\omega_i^2\|h^i\|^2.
\]
Moreover, $h^i$ is the orthogonal-projection residual of
$\nabla f(x^i)$, so $\|h^i\|\le\|\nabla f(x^i)\|$.  Telescoping and using
\eqref{eq:algorithm-gradient} now give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:aggregate-interval}
 \|z^k\|^2-\|z^{\ell-1}\|^2
 =\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2\|h^i\|^2
 \le3\mathcal L\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2d_i.
\end{equation}
Split the decrease sum on the left of
\eqref{eq:weighted-gap-identity} into three quarters and one quarter.
By \eqref{eq:aggregate-interval}, the latter quarter is at least
$(\|z^k\|^2-\|z^{\ell-1}\|^2)/(12\mathcal L)$.  Moving this lower bound to
the right proves \eqref{eq:window-reserve}.
head: environment

label: lem:prefix
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Prefix estimates

label: eq:prefix-complete-square
title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:reserve} with $\ell=0$.  The conventions
$\omega_{-1}=0$ and $z^{-1}=0$, together with $e^0=0$, reduce its right-hand
side to
\[
 (x^0-x^\star)^Tz^k-\frac{\|z^k\|^2}{12\mathcal L}
 +D_0\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_i\|e^i\|.
\]
Completing the square gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prefix-complete-square}
 (x^0-x^\star)^Tz^k-\frac{\|z^k\|^2}{12\mathcal L}
 =3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2
  -\frac{\|z^k-6\mathcal L(x^0-x^\star)\|^2}{12\mathcal L}
 \le3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2.
\end{equation}

We use the following elementary scalar inequality.  For
$\alpha\ge0$, $\beta>0$, and $t\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-young}
 \alpha t^{2/3}-\beta t\le\frac{4\alpha^3}{27\beta^2}.
\end{equation}
To verify it, write $t=y^3$ with $y\ge0$.  The derivative of
$\alpha y^2-\beta y^3$ is $y(2\alpha-3\beta y)$, so the maximum is attained
at $y=2\alpha/(3\beta)$ (or at $y=0$ if $\alpha=0$), and its value is the
right-hand side of \eqref{eq:weighted-young}.

For $i\ge1$, the defect estimate \eqref{eq:defect-budget} and
\eqref{eq:weighted-young}, with
\[
 \alpha=D_0(18H)^{1/3}\omega_i,\qquad
 \beta=\frac{\omega_{i-1}^2}{2},\qquad
 t=d_{i-1},
\]
give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prefix-defect-young}
 D_0\omega_i\|e^i\|-\frac12\omega_{i-1}^2d_{i-1}
 \le\frac{32}{3}HD_0^3
       \frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}.
\end{equation}
After summing \eqref{eq:prefix-defect-young} from $i=1$ to $k$, the
decrease left after this absorption is at least one quarter of the whole
prefix, because
\[
 \frac34\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 -\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_{i-1}^2d_{i-1}
 =\frac14\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\omega_i^2d_i
  +\frac34\omega_k^2d_k
 \ge\frac14\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i.
\]

The bounds in \eqref{eq:weights} imply, for $i\ge1$,
\[
 \frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}
 \le\frac{(i+1)^3}{((i+1)/2)^4}
 =\frac{16}{i+1}.
\]
For $k\ge1$, monotonicity of $u\mapsto1/u$ gives
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{i+1}
 \le\int_1^{k+1}\frac{du}{u}=\log(k+1);
\]
for $k=0$ both sides of the corresponding empty-sum estimate are zero.
Combining this bound with \eqref{eq:window-reserve},
\eqref{eq:prefix-complete-square}, and
\eqref{eq:prefix-defect-young} proves the first inequality in
\eqref{eq:window-prefix}.  The second follows from the definition
\eqref{eq:proof-scale}.

Equation \eqref{eq:aggregate-interval} with $\ell=0$, followed by
\eqref{eq:window-prefix}, gives
\[
 \|z^k\|^2
 \le3\mathcal L\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 \le12\mathcal L C_{\mathrm{global}}(1+\log(k+1)),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:window-aggregate-bound}.

It remains to prove \eqref{eq:prefix-gap}.  Convexity and
\eqref{eq:algorithm-gradient} give
\[
 \Delta_0
 \le\|x^0-x^\star\|\,\|\nabla f(x^0)\|,
 \qquad
 \|\nabla f(x^0)\|^2\le3\mathcal L d_0
 \le3\mathcal L\Delta_0.
\]
If $\Delta_0=0$, the first assertion is immediate.  Otherwise, divide the
combined inequality by $\sqrt{\Delta_0}$ and square to obtain
$\Delta_0\le3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2$.

For $\ell=1$, this initial estimate and \eqref{eq:proof-scale} imply
$\Delta_0\le C_{\mathrm{global}}\le4C_{\mathrm{global}}(1+\log1)$.  If $\ell\ge2$, use
\eqref{eq:window-prefix} with $k=\ell-2$ and the weight lower bound
$\omega_{\ell-2}\ge \ell/2$:
\[
 \Delta_{\ell-1}
 \le\frac{C_{\mathrm{global}}(1+\log(\ell-1))}{\omega_{\ell-2}^2}
 \le\frac{4C_{\mathrm{global}}(1+\log \ell)}{\ell^2}.
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:window
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Comparable-weight window

label: eq:window-ratio-sum
title: Proof
body_md:
The lower weight bound in \eqref{eq:weights} shows that the defining index
$k$ exists.  Since $\omega_{\ell-1}\ge1$ and the weight recurrence gives the
strict inequality $\omega_\ell<\omega_{\ell-1}+1\le2\omega_{\ell-1}$, we have
$k\ge \ell+1$.  By minimality, $\omega_{k-1}<2\omega_{\ell-1}$.  The increment
bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:weights} therefore give
\[
 \omega_{\ell-1}+\frac{k-\ell}{2}
 \le\omega_{k-1}<2\omega_{\ell-1},
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad k-\ell<2\omega_{\ell-1}.
\]
For $\ell<i\le k$, we also have
$\omega_{i-1}\ge\omega_{\ell-1}$ and
$\omega_i\le\omega_{i-1}+1\le2\omega_{i-1}$.  Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:window-ratio-sum}
 \sum_{i=\ell+1}^k\frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}
 \le\sum_{i=\ell+1}^k\frac{8}{\omega_{i-1}}
 \le\frac{8(k-\ell)}{\omega_{\ell-1}}
 \le16.
\end{equation}

We first bound the aggregate boundary term in Lemma~\ref{lem:reserve}.
The Pythagorean identity in \eqref{eq:aggregate-interval} shows that
$\|z^k\|\ge\|z^{\ell-1}\|$.  Put
$t=\|z^k\|-\|z^{\ell-1}\|\ge0$.  The triangle inequality gives
$\|z^k-z^{\ell-1}\|\le2\|z^{\ell-1}\|+t$, while
\[
 \|z^k\|^2-\|z^{\ell-1}\|^2
 =2\|z^{\ell-1}\|t+t^2.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 &(x^0-x^\star)^T(z^k-z^{\ell-1})
 -\frac{\|z^k\|^2-\|z^{\ell-1}\|^2}{12\mathcal L}\\
 &\quad\le
 2\|x^0-x^\star\|\,\|z^{\ell-1}\|
 +\left(\|x^0-x^\star\|-\frac{\|z^{\ell-1}\|}{6\mathcal L}\right)t
 -\frac{t^2}{12\mathcal L}\\
 &\quad\le
 2\|x^0-x^\star\|\,\|z^{\ell-1}\|
 +3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2.
\end{align*}
For the last line, the maximum over $t\ge0$ of the last two terms is
\[
 3\mathcal L
 \max\!\left\{\|x^0-x^\star\|-
       \frac{\|z^{\ell-1}\|}{6\mathcal L},0\right\}^2
 \le3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:window-aggregate-bound} with $k=\ell-1$ and
$3\mathcal L\|x^0-x^\star\|^2\le C_{\mathrm{global}}$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:window-boundary}
\begin{aligned}
 &(x^0-x^\star)^T(z^k-z^{\ell-1})
 -\frac{\|z^k\|^2-\|z^{\ell-1}\|^2}{12\mathcal L}\\
 &\qquad\le
 4C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}+C_{\mathrm{global}}
 \le5C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The bound for $e^\ell$ uses $d_{\ell-1}$, the decrease immediately
before the current interval.  Since
$d_{\ell-1}\le\Delta_{\ell-1}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix},
$\omega_\ell\le \ell+1\le2\ell$, and \eqref{eq:defect-budget} give
\begin{align*}
 D_0\omega_\ell\|e^\ell\|
 &\le2D_0(18H)^{1/3}\ell
       \left(\frac{4C_{\mathrm{global}}(1+\log \ell)}{\ell^2}\right)^{2/3}\\
 &=2\,4^{2/3}D_0(18H)^{1/3}C_{\mathrm{global}}^{2/3}
       \left(\frac{(1+\log \ell)^2}{\ell}\right)^{1/3}.
\end{align*}
The definition of $C_{\mathrm{global}}$ implies
\[
 \bigl[D_0(18H)^{1/3}\bigr]^3
 =18HD_0^3\le\frac{27}{256}C_{\mathrm{global}}.
\]
The function $v\mapsto(1+\log v)^2/v$ on $[1,\infty)$ has derivative
$(1+\log v)(1-\log v)/v^2$, and hence its maximum is $4/e$, attained at
$v=e$.  Substitution gives the explicit bound
\begin{equation}\label{eq:first-window-defect}
 D_0\omega_\ell\|e^\ell\|
 \le(54/e)^{1/3}C_{\mathrm{global}}<4C_{\mathrm{global}}.
\end{equation}

Every remaining correction is paid for inside the current window.  For
$\ell<i\le k$, the same scalar inequality \eqref{eq:weighted-young} used in
the prefix proof gives
\[
 D_0\omega_i\|e^i\|-\frac12\omega_{i-1}^2d_{i-1}
 \le\frac{32}{3}HD_0^3
       \frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}.
\]
Summing and using \eqref{eq:window-ratio-sum} bounds the unabsorbed part by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:internal-window-defects}
 \frac{32}{3}HD_0^3
 \sum_{i=\ell+1}^k\frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}
 \le\frac{512}{3}HD_0^3\le C_{\mathrm{global}}.
\end{equation}
The absorbed decreases are precisely those indexed from $\ell$ through
$k-1$.  Hence the decrease remaining on the left of
\eqref{eq:window-reserve} satisfies
\[
 \frac34\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 -\frac12\sum_{i=\ell+1}^k\omega_{i-1}^2d_{i-1}
 =\frac14\sum_{i=\ell}^{k-1}\omega_i^2d_i
  +\frac34\omega_k^2d_k
 \ge\frac14\sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2d_i.
\]
Finally, combine \eqref{eq:window-boundary},
\eqref{eq:first-window-defect}, and
\eqref{eq:internal-window-defects}.  Since
$\sqrt{1+\log \ell}\ge1$, their sum is at most
\[
 5C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}+4C_{\mathrm{global}}+C_{\mathrm{global}}
 \le10C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}
 \le16C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:window-reserve} proves
\eqref{eq:window-gap-recurrence}.

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian},
Algorithm~\ref{alg:cubic}, with exact model solves and projections,
is well defined and generates a monotone sequence in $\mathcal C_0$.
If $\nabla f(x^0)\ne0$, then for every $K\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicit-rate}
 f(x^K)-f_\star\le
 \frac{2048\left[3\bigl(L_0+\sqrt{2HL_0D_0}\bigr)\|x^0-x^\star\|^2
                    +\tfrac{512}{3}HD_0^3\right]
                  \sqrt{1+\log(K+1)}}{(K+1)^2},
\end{equation}

Consequently, for a universal constant $C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-rate}
 f(x^K)-f_\star\le C(L_0D_0^2+HD_0^3)
             \frac{\sqrt{1+\log(K+1)}}{(K+1)^2}.
\end{equation}
The same claims hold trivially for a stationary initial point and
after constant extension following finite termination.
head: environment
name: Global convergence with three HVPs

title: Proof
body_md:
Propositions~\ref{prop:iteration} and~\ref{prop:oracles} give
well-definedness, monotonicity, and the oracle count.
If $\nabla f(x^0)=0$, convexity makes $x^0$ a minimizer and there
is nothing to prove. Otherwise the preceding lemmas apply.
Recall that $\Delta_k=f(x^k)-f_\star$, $d_k=\Delta_k-\Delta_{k+1}$,
and that the bracket in \eqref{eq:explicit-rate} is the constant
$C_{\mathrm{global}}$ in \eqref{eq:proof-scale}.

Partition the positive indices into the intervals of
Lemma~\ref{lem:window}. Set $k_0=1$. For each interval number
$j\ge0$, let $k_{j+1}$ be one plus the first index at least $k_j$
for which $\omega_{k_{j+1}-1}\ge2\omega_{k_j-1}$.
Thus interval $j$ consists of the steps $k_j,\ldots,k_{j+1}-1$.
To track the weighted gap at its beginning, define
\[
 U_j=\omega_{k_j-1}^2\Delta_{k_j}.
\]
These intervals cover all positive indices because the weights
increase without bound.

For one such interval, write $\ell=k_j$ and $k=k_{j+1}-1$.
Monotonicity of the weights and telescoping of the decreases give
\[
 \sum_{i=\ell}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 \ge\omega_\ell^2\sum_{i=\ell}^k d_i
 =\omega_\ell^2(\Delta_\ell-\Delta_{k+1}).
\]
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:window-gap-recurrence} yields
\[
 \left(\omega_k^2-\tfrac14\omega_\ell^2\right)\Delta_{k+1}
 \le\left(\omega_{\ell-1}^2-\tfrac14\omega_\ell^2\right)\Delta_\ell
            +16C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log \ell}.
\]
For the following algebra only, put
\[
 \alpha=\frac{\omega_\ell^2}{\omega_{\ell-1}^2},\qquad
 \beta=\frac{\omega_k^2}{\omega_{\ell-1}^2}.
\]
The weight increment bound and $\omega_{\ell-1}\ge1$ give
$1\le \alpha<4$, while the definition of $k$ gives $\beta\ge4$.
As $U_{j+1}=\omega_k^2\Delta_{k+1}$, the preceding inequality is
\[
 U_{j+1}\le
 \frac{1-\alpha/4}{1-\alpha/(4\beta)}U_j
 +\frac{16C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log k_j}}{1-\alpha/(4\beta)}.
\]
Both coefficients can be bounded independently of the interval.
Indeed,
\[
 \frac{1-\alpha/4}{1-\alpha/(4\beta)}
 \le\frac{1-\alpha/4}{1-\alpha/16}\le\frac45,
 \qquad
 \frac1{1-\alpha/(4\beta)}\le\frac43.
\]
For the second inequality in the first chain, the rational function
decreases for $1\le \alpha<4$, so its maximum is attained at $\alpha=1$.
We have therefore obtained the contraction
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-contraction}
 U_{j+1}\le\frac45U_j+22C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log k_j}.
\end{equation}

The initial value satisfies
$U_0=\Delta_1\le\Delta_0\le C_{\mathrm{global}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix}.
Induction in \eqref{eq:endpoint-contraction}, using $k_{j+1}>k_j$,
gives
\[
 U_j\le110C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log k_j}.
\]
The constant $110$ is chosen so that $(4/5)110+22=110$.
For an arbitrary $K\ge1$, choose the interval containing it,
$k_j\le K<k_{j+1}$. By monotonicity, $\Delta_K\le\Delta_{k_j}$.
The defining minimality of $k_{j+1}-1$ gives
$\omega_{K-1}<2\omega_{k_j-1}$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:weights} gives $\omega_{K-1}\ge(K+1)/2$.
Combining these relations,
\begin{align*}
 \Delta_K
 &\le\frac{U_j}{\omega_{k_j-1}^2}
 \le\frac{16U_j}{(K+1)^2}\\
 &\le\frac{1760C_{\mathrm{global}}\sqrt{1+\log(K+1)}}{(K+1)^2}.
\end{align*}
For $K=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix} gives $\Delta_0\le C_{\mathrm{global}}$.
Thus the uniform factor $2048$ in \eqref{eq:explicit-rate} covers
all indices. At any terminating index the gap becomes zero, so
constant extension preserves the estimate.

Finally, $\|x^0-x^\star\|\le D_0$ and the elementary inequality
$\sqrt{ab}\le(a+b)/2$ give
\[
 \mathcal L D_0^2
 =L_0D_0^2+\sqrt{2(L_0D_0^2)(HD_0^3)}
 \le\tfrac32L_0D_0^2+HD_0^3.
\]
Absorbing the numerical constants proves \eqref{eq:main-rate}.
head: environment

label: ass:local
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:local}
The Hessian at the fixed minimizer $x^\star$ is positive definite:
\[
 v^T\nabla^2f(x^\star)v>0\qquad\text{for every }v\ne0.
\]
head: environment
name: Nondegenerate minimizer

label: lem:local-entry
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-entry}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}, \ref{ass:level},
\ref{ass:hessian}, and~\ref{ass:local}, the minimizer $x^\star$
is unique and the iterates of Algorithm~\ref{alg:cubic} converge
to it. In particular, for all sufficiently large $k$,
\[
 \nabla^2f(x^k)\succeq\tfrac12\mu_\star I.
\]
head: environment
name: The iterates enter the local region

title: Proof
body_md:
Continuity of the Hessian gives a ball about $x^\star$ on which
$\nabla^2f(x)\succeq(\mu_\star/2)I$. Since
$\nabla f(x^\star)=0$, integrating along the segment from $x^\star$
to a point in that ball gives
\[
 f(x)\ge f(x^\star)+\tfrac14\mu_\star\|x-x^\star\|^2.
\]
Thus $x^\star$ is a strict local minimizer. If a second global
minimizer existed, convexity would make every point of the segment
between the two a minimizer. Points on that segment arbitrarily
close to $x^\star$ would contradict the displayed inequality.
Hence the global minimizer is unique.

Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives $f(x^k)\to f(x^\star)$, and all
iterates lie in the compact initial sublevel $\mathcal C_0$.
By continuity, every cluster point must therefore be a global
minimizer and so must equal $x^\star$. This implies convergence
of the whole sequence: otherwise some subsequence would remain
a positive distance from $x^\star$, while compactness would give
it a cluster point with that same property. The Hessian bound now
follows from entry into the ball chosen above.
head: environment

label: lem:local-projection
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The error after one model step

label: eq:local-gradient-expansion
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $u^k=x^k-x^\star$. The initial sublevel is convex and
contains both $x^k$ and $x^\star$. Assumption~\ref{ass:hessian}
therefore applies along their segment. In particular,
\begin{align}
 \|\nabla f(x^k)-\nabla^2f(x^\star)u^k\|
 &\le\int_0^1 2Ht\|u^k\|^2\,dt
 =H\|u^k\|^2,\label{eq:local-gradient-expansion}\\
 \|\nabla^2f(x^k)-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\|&\le2H\|u^k\|.
 \label{eq:local-hessian-expansion}
\end{align}
The first bound also gives
$\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\le L_\star\|u^k\|+H\|u^k\|^2=O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star)$.

Since $s^k\in\mathcal S^k$, taking its inner product with the
projected stationarity equation~\eqref{eq:model-stationarity}
gives
\[
 (s^k)^T\nabla^2f(x^k)s^k+H\|s^k\|^3
 =-\nabla f(x^k)^Ts^k.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-entry} and Cauchy--Schwarz imply
\[
 \tfrac12\mu_\star\|s^k\|^2
 \le\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\|s^k\|,
 \qquad
 \|s^k\|\le\frac{2}{\mu_\star}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|=O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star).
\]
The last inequality also holds when $s^k=0$.

Define the stationarity remainder
\[
 r^k=\nabla^2f(x^\star)u^k-\nabla f(x^k)
       +(\nabla^2f(x^\star)-\nabla^2f(x^k))s^k-H\|s^k\|s^k.
\]
The two Taylor bounds and the step-length estimate yield
\[
 \|r^k\|
 \le H\|u^k\|^2+2H\|u^k\|\|s^k\|+H\|s^k\|^2
 =O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2).
\]
For every $v\in\mathcal S^k$, equation~\eqref{eq:model-stationarity}
now gives
\[
 v^T\nabla^2f(x^\star)(u^k+s^k)=v^Tr^k.
\]
By the defining property of the projector orthogonal in the norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$,
$P^k(u^k+s^k)=P^k[\nabla^2f(x^\star)]^{-1}r^k$.
Also $(I-P^k)s^k=0$, because $s^k$ lies in the search space.
Together these identities prove~\eqref{eq:local-projection} with
$w^k=P^k[\nabla^2f(x^\star)]^{-1}r^k$. Orthogonal projection does not increase
the norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$, so
\[
 \|w^k\|_\star\le\|[\nabla^2f(x^\star)]^{-1}r^k\|_\star
 \le \mu_\star^{-1/2}\|r^k\|=O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2).
\]
All estimates are uniform for sufficiently large $k$, independently
of the dimension of $\mathcal S^k$ or the angles between its defining directions.
Finally, $(I-P^k)u^k$ is the error of the best approximation from
$\mathcal S^k$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$. The triangle inequality in
\eqref{eq:local-projection} gives~\eqref{eq:local-distance-bound}.
head: environment

label: thm:local
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:local}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}, \ref{ass:level},
\ref{ass:hessian}, and~\ref{ass:local}, the iterates converge to $x^\star$. Unless the method terminates
finitely, there is a finite constant $C$ such that, eventually,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-rate}
 \|x^{k+1}-x^\star\|_\star\le\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1} \|x^k-x^\star\|_\star+C\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2.
\end{equation}
For every $q\in(\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1},1)$, this gives
$\|x^{k+1}-x^\star\|_\star\le q\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star$ for all sufficiently large $k$. In the absence
of finite termination, the objective gaps also satisfy
\[
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \frac{f(x^{k+1})-f_\star}{f(x^k)-f_\star}
 \le\left(\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1}\right)^2.
\]
No strong-convexity parameter, restart, or test for entering a local
phase is supplied to the algorithm.
head: environment
name: Local linear rate without a supplied modulus

title: Proof
body_md:
Convergence follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:local-entry}.
Because $\nabla f(x^k)\in\mathcal S^k$, we can approximate
$u^k=x^k-x^\star$ by
$2\nabla f(x^k)/(L_\star+\mu_\star)$ inside that space.
The approximation error is
\[
 u^k-\frac{2\nabla f(x^k)}{L_\star+\mu_\star}
 =\left(I-\frac{2\nabla^2f(x^\star)}{L_\star+\mu_\star}\right)u^k
   +\frac{2(\nabla^2f(x^\star)u^k-\nabla f(x^k))}{L_\star+\mu_\star}.
\]
The second term has size $O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2)$
in the norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$, by
\eqref{eq:local-gradient-expansion} and equivalence of the norms.
For the first term, diagonalize $\nabla^2f(x^\star)$. A component corresponding to
an eigenvalue $\lambda\in[\mu_\star,L_\star]$ is multiplied by
$1-2\lambda/(L_\star+\mu_\star)$, whose absolute value is at most
$\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1}$. Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{dist}_\star(u^k,\mathcal S^k)
 &\le\left\|u^k-\frac{2\nabla f(x^k)}{L_\star+\mu_\star}\right\|_\star\\
 &\le\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1} \|x^k-x^\star\|_\star+O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Combining this with Lemma~\ref{lem:local-projection} proves
\eqref{eq:local-rate}. Given $q>\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1}$, convergence ensures
$C\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star\le q-\frac{\kappa_\star-1}{\kappa_\star+1}$ eventually; dividing
\eqref{eq:local-rate} by $\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star$ then gives the claimed contraction.

Finally, the Hessian Lipschitz bound on the segment from $x^\star$
to $x^k$ gives the two-sided Taylor estimate
\[
 \left|f(x^k)-f_\star-\tfrac12\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2\right|
 \le\tfrac H3\|x^k-x^\star\|^3=O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^3).
\]
Thus the objective gap is $\tfrac12\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2(1+O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star))$.
Substituting~\eqref{eq:local-rate} into the ratio of consecutive
gaps proves the last assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:local-pl
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Local PL convergence and finite trajectory length

title: Proof
body_md:
Within the proof, write
\[
 C_{\mathrm{grad}}=3(L_0+\sqrt{2HL_0D_0}),\qquad
 c_{\mathrm{step}}=2H/3.
\]
The argument uses only the two decrease bounds with these positive
coefficients. It therefore also applies when other variants supply
different positive coefficients, with $q=1-2\mu/C_{\mathrm{grad}}$.
Summing the first bound gives
$\sum_k\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2<\infty$. All accumulation points are
therefore stationary, hence minimize $f$ by convexity. Compactness,
continuity, and monotonicity imply $f(x^k)\to f_\star$.
Write $\Delta_k=f(x^k)-f_\star$ within this proof.
At an iterate in the PL neighborhood, the two bounds give
\[
 \Delta_{k+1}\le q\Delta_k,\qquad
 \|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\le c_{\mathrm{step}}^{-1/3}\Delta_k^{1/3}.
\]
Choose an index $k_0$ along a subsequence converging to $\bar x$
such that
\[
 \|x^{k_0}-\bar x\|
 +\frac{\Delta_{k_0}^{1/3}}
       {c_{\mathrm{step}}^{1/3}(1-q^{1/3})}<r.
\]
If $x^K$ were the first subsequent iterate outside the ball, the
contraction holds at every preceding iterate, including $x^{K-1}$.
Consequently
\[
 \|x^K-\bar x\|
 \le\|x^{k_0}-\bar x\|
 +c_{\mathrm{step}}^{-1/3}\Delta_{k_0}^{1/3}
       \sum_{i=k_0}^{K-1}q^{(i-k_0)/3}<r,
\]
a contradiction. This proves invariance even if an individual
trial segment is not assumed to lie in the PL neighborhood.
Summing the step bound from any later $k$ proves the finite-length
estimate. The sequence is Cauchy, and its limit must equal its
accumulation point $\bar x$. The remaining estimate follows from
the geometric gap bound.
head: environment

label: lem:epoch-bound
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: An epoch with an arbitrary initial weight

title: Proof
body_md:
Abbreviate $\mathcal L=L_0+\sqrt{2HL_0D_0}$ within this proof.
If $\nabla f(y^0)=0$, constant extension gives both estimates
immediately. Otherwise $\mathcal L>0$ by
\eqref{eq:gradient-level-bound}. Gradient inclusion gives
monotonicity and invariance by Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance}.
Moreover,
\[
 y^{i+1}-y^0=(y^i-y^0)+s^i\in\mathcal S^i,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{span}\{y^{i+1}-y^0,z^i\}\subseteq\mathcal S^i.
\]
Thus the one-step bounds \eqref{eq:global-two-budgets} and the
corrected-gradient orthogonalities remain valid with $y^0$ as the epoch's starting point.
None of these facts requires the incoming displacement to be zero.

For this proof, write
\[
 \Delta_i=f(y^i)-f_\star,\qquad
 d_i=f(y^i)-f(y^{i+1})\ge0,
\]
and let $h^i$ and $e^i$ denote the corrected gradient and the
removed component within this epoch. Set
$h^0=\nabla f(y^0)$, $e^0=0$, and $z^{-1}=0$.
The weight recurrence gives
\[
 \omega_i^2-\omega_{i-1}^2=\omega_i\quad(i\ge1),
 \qquad
 t+\frac i2\le\omega_i\le t+i.
\]
The increment bounds follow from the same calculation as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:weights}. Telescoping the difference identity gives
$\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i=\omega_k^2-t^2+t$.
Consequently, summation by parts yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:epoch-gap-identity}
 \omega_k^2\Delta_{k+1}
 +\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 =(t^2-t)\Delta_0+\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i\Delta_i.
\end{equation}
This is the only change to the starting boundary term in
\eqref{eq:weighted-gap-identity}.

As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:reserve}, convexity and
$(h^i)^T(y^i-y^0)=0$ imply
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i\Delta_i
 \le(y^0-x^\star)^Tz^k
      +D_0\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_i\|e^i\|.
\]
The orthogonality $(h^i)^Tz^{i-1}=0$ gives
\[
 \|z^k\|^2
 =\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2\|h^i\|^2
 \le3\mathcal L\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i.
\]
Use half of the weighted decrease in
\eqref{eq:epoch-gap-identity} to bound the aggregate. Completing
the square gives
\begin{align*}
 \omega_k^2\Delta_{k+1}
 +\frac12\sum_{i=0}^k\omega_i^2d_i
 &\le(t^2-t)\Delta_0+(y^0-x^\star)^Tz^k
       -\frac{\|z^k\|^2}{6\mathcal L}
       +D_0\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_i\|e^i\|\\
 &\le(t^2-t)\Delta_0
       +\frac32\mathcal L\|y^0-x^\star\|^2
       +D_0\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_i\|e^i\|.
\end{align*}
The remaining half of the decrease pays for the correction errors.
Indeed, the defect bound and \eqref{eq:weighted-young} give
\[
 D_0\omega_i\|e^i\|
 -\frac12\omega_{i-1}^2d_{i-1}
 \le\frac{32}{3}HD_0^3
       \frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}
 \qquad(i\ge1).
\]
Summing this inequality and discarding the remaining nonnegative
term $\omega_k^2d_k/2$ proves \eqref{eq:epoch-bound}.

For a completed epoch, $k=4t$ and $\omega_{4t}\ge3t$.
Since $\omega_{i-1}\ge t\ge1$ and
$\omega_i\le\omega_{i-1}+1\le2\omega_{i-1}$,
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{4t}\frac{\omega_i^3}{\omega_{i-1}^4}
 \le\sum_{i=1}^{4t}\frac8{\omega_{i-1}}
 \le32.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:epoch-bound} proves
\eqref{eq:completed-epoch}.
head: environment

label: thm:restarted-rate
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Inverse-square convergence with deterministic epochs

title: Proof
body_md:
For this induction, abbreviate the numerator of
\eqref{eq:restarted-rate} by
\[
 C_{\mathrm{restart}}=81D_0^2
 \left[\tfrac32\bigl(L_0+\sqrt{2HL_0D_0}\bigr)
                      +\tfrac{1024}{3}HD_0\right].
\]
Gradient inclusion is preserved at every restart, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance} gives monotonicity and invariance
throughout the run. If a zero gradient is encountered, constant
extension preserves the claimed bound and requires no further
oracle calls. We therefore prove the estimate on the remaining
nonstationary trajectory.

The completed-epoch bound has additive term
$C_{\mathrm{restart}}/81$, where $C_{\mathrm{restart}}$ is the numerator
of the stated rate.
Suppose an epoch with initial weight $t$ starts at $y^0$ with
$f(y^0)-f_\star\le C_{\mathrm{restart}}/(81t^2)$. Then
\eqref{eq:completed-epoch} gives
\[
 f(y^{4t+1})-f_\star
 \le\frac{(t^2-t)C_{\mathrm{restart}}/(81t^2)+(C_{\mathrm{restart}}/81)}{9t^2}
 \le\frac{2(C_{\mathrm{restart}}/81)}{9t^2}
 \le\frac{C_{\mathrm{restart}}}{81(2t)^2}.
\]
This is the required starting estimate for the next epoch.
For the first epoch, $t=1$. Integrating the Hessian on the segment
from $x^\star$ to $x^0$ gives
\[
 f(x^0)-f_\star
 \le\frac{L_0}{2}\|x^0-x^\star\|^2
 \le\frac{L_0D_0^2}{2}\le C_{\mathrm{restart}}/81.
\]
Induction proves the starting estimate in every epoch. Neither the gap nor $C_{\mathrm{restart}}$ is used by the algorithm.

Let $\tau_j$ be the global index at the start of epoch $j$.
Summing the preceding epoch lengths gives
\[
 \tau_j=\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}(4\cdot2^\ell+1)
       =4(2^j-1)+j.
\]
If $\tau_j\le K<\tau_{j+1}$ and $t=2^j$, monotonicity and the
starting estimate give $f(x^K)-f_\star\le C_{\mathrm{restart}}/(81t^2)$.
Moreover,
\[
 K+1\le\tau_{j+1}=8t+j-3\le9t,
\]
where $j\le2^j=t$ for every integer $j\ge0$.
Thus $f(x^K)-f_\star\le C_{\mathrm{restart}}/(K+1)^2$, which is
\eqref{eq:restarted-rate}.

Each restarted space has at most three dimensions. Forming its
reduced Hessian and updating the gradient therefore has the same
oracle count as Proposition~\ref{prop:oracles}. Restarting uses
the current gradient already in memory and requires no additional
oracle call.

Finally, under Assumption~\ref{ass:local}, the minimizer is unique
by the argument in Lemma~\ref{lem:local-entry}. Compactness and
\eqref{eq:restarted-rate} imply $x^K\to x^\star$. The local
projection estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:local-projection} and the
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:local} use only gradient inclusion,
the fixed cubic coefficient, and the local Hessian bounds. They
do not depend on a fixed epoch starting point or aggregate. They consequently
apply across the epoch boundaries and give the same local rate.
head: environment

label: thm:oracle-lower-bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:oracle-lower-bound}
 
A vector-oracle call returns either $\nabla f(x)$ or
$\nabla^2f(x)v$. Consider algorithms starting at $0$ for which every
query point, HVP input vector, and output point belongs to the linear
span of previously returned vectors; before the first call this span
is $\{0\}$. Scalar coefficients may depend arbitrarily on the observed
information. Memory, scalar computations, and function-value queries
within the available span are unrestricted. Every gradient or HVP
evaluation counts, including the initial gradient and any inner calls.

For every integer call budget $M\ge1$, there exists a convex nonquadratic
$C^\infty$ function $f:\mathbb R^{M+2}\to\mathbb R$ with compact sublevel sets
and a unique minimizer $x^\star$, such that
\[
 0\preceq\nabla^2f(x)\preceq3I\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^{M+2}).
\]
Its smallest global Hessian Lipschitz constant is exactly $2$,
so $H=1$ is a valid supplied bound. Its third derivative is globally
$32$-Lipschitz in the induced multilinear norm. For
$\mathcal C_0=\{x:f(x)\le f(0)\}$, the level-set constants are
\[
 L_0=\max_{x\in\mathcal C_0}\|\nabla^2f(x)\|=1,
 \qquad D_0=\max_{x\in\mathcal C_0}\|x-x^\star\|=1.
\]
On this single function, every algorithm in the stated class and
every output $x$ obtained after at most $M$ vector-oracle calls satisfy
\[
 f(x)-f_\star\ge\frac{1}{2\cosh^2(2)(M+1)^2},
 \qquad f_\star=f(x^\star).
\]
Monotonicity is not required. In particular, a uniformly bounded
number of gradient and HVP calls per outer iteration cannot yield
a uniform dimension-independent $O(k^{-3})$ guarantee with constants
depending only on the displayed smoothness and level-set bounds.
head: environment
name: Adapted classical Krylov lower bound

label: lem:local-epoch
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-epoch}
Start an epoch at $y\in\mathcal C_0$, with initial weight $t\ge1$
and aggregate $t\nabla f(y)$. Perform $4t+1$ steps, where $t$ is an
integer, and denote the endpoint by $y^+$.
Suppose the current sublevel set
$\mathcal C(y)=\{x:f(x)\le f(y)\}$ is contained in a neighborhood
where $\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq\mu I$, with $\mu>0$. Define
\[
 D=\max_{x\in\mathcal C(y)}\|x-x^\star\|,\qquad
 L=\max_{x\in\mathcal C(y)}\|\nabla^2 f(x)\|.
\]
Here $D$ is the radius of the current sublevel and $L$ is its
Hessian norm bound. For $\Delta=f(y)-f_\star$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-epoch-factor}
 f(y^+)-f_\star
 \le
 \frac{t^2-t+3\bigl(L+\sqrt{4HLD}\bigr)/\mu
                 +(4096/3)HD/\mu}{9t^2}\,\Delta.
\end{equation}

the epoch.

the corrected-gradient orthogonalities relative to the epoch's
starting point, and the local decrease bounds. It does not require that
the incoming displacement be zero. Apply it on $\mathcal C(y)$,

body_md:
\label{thm:automatic-acceleration}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian}, use exact
fixed-coefficient steps or the adaptive steps of Section~\ref{sec:adaptive}.
Apply the preceding controller and index its single
trajectory by the total number $K$ of accepted cubic steps.
The trajectory is monotone, stays in $\mathcal C_0$, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:controlled-global-rate}
 f(x^K)-f_\star\le\frac{5184D_0^2}{(K+1)^2}
 \left[\frac32\bigl(L_0+\sqrt{4HL_0D_0}\bigr)
                    +\frac{2048}{3}HD_0\right]
 \qquad(K\ge0).
\end{equation}
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:local}, with $\kappa_\star$ defined above,
$x^K\to x^\star$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:controlled-local-root}
 \limsup_{K\to\infty}(f(x^K)-f_\star)^{1/K}
 \le \exp\left(-\frac{\log 2}{116\sqrt{\kappa_\star}}\right).
\end{equation}
For a positive initial gap, reducing it by a factor $\varepsilon$
requires at most
\[
 \left(\frac{116\sqrt{\kappa_\star}}{\log2}+o(1)\right)
 \log(1/\varepsilon)
 \qquad\text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0,
\]
where the $o(1)$ is for the fixed problem.

\[
 d_{J-2}\le2^{-(J-2)}d_0
 \le2^{-(J-2)}\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}.
\]

\[
 \Delta_{\mathrm{end}}
 \le\frac{d_{J-2}}{\theta}
 \le\frac4\theta\,2^{-J}\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}.
\]
For $J=1$ the same bound follows from monotonicity and $\theta<1$.

than assigning length $\ell_{\max}$ to every epoch.

completed epochs, and let its logarithmic gap reduction be
\[
 G_\ell=\log_2
 \frac{\text{gap before these epochs}}{\text{gap after these epochs}}.
\]

For a level with no completed epoch, set $J_\ell=G_\ell=0$.

 \sum_{\ell=0}^R(4\cdot2^\ell+1)
 =8t_\star+R-3\le3\ell_{\max},

 &\le3\ell_{\max}\log_2(4/\theta)

 \end{aligned}

\end{equation}

$\beta$ is the progress exponent within a tuned stage. Both are
analysis constants; the controller uses neither.

body_md:
The entry index is $\lceil8\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{restart}}/
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}}\rceil$, using the numerator abbreviation
from the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:automatic-acceleration}.
Set $\rho=\mu_\star/(4096H)$ and
$L_\star=\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(x^\star))$.
For $x\in\mathcal C_0$ with $\|x-x^\star\|\le\rho$, the Hessian
Lipschitz bound gives
\[
 \|\nabla^2 f(x)-\nabla^2 f(x^\star)\|
 \le2H\rho\le\frac{\mu_\star}{1024}.
\]
In particular, the Hessian there is bounded below by
$(\mu_\star/2)I$ and above by $2L_\star I$.
If a point $x\in\mathcal C_0$ lies at distance at least $\rho$
from $x^\star$, its segment to $x^\star$ lies in the convex set
$\mathcal C_0$. At the first point $z$ on that segment at distance
$\rho$ from $x^\star$, integration of the Hessian lower bound gives
$f(z)-f_\star\ge \mu_\star\rho^2/4$.
Convexity along the ray implies $f(x)\ge f(z)$. Since
$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mu_\star\rho^2/8$, we have proved
\[
 \mathcal C_0\cap\{x:f(x)-f_\star\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}\}
 \subset B(x^\star,\rho).
\]
Only segments inside $\mathcal C_0$ were used; the full ball need
not lie in that set.

On this local sublevel, take $\mu=\mu_\star/2$ and let $D$ be the
maximum distance to $x^\star$, so that $D\le\rho$.
The constants in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:automatic-acceleration} then satisfy
\[
 2L_\star+\sqrt{8HL_\star D}\le3L_\star,\qquad
 \frac{4096HD}{3\mu}\le\frac23\le\kappa_\star.
\]
Substitution into Lemma~\ref{lem:local-epoch} and the first-step
decrease bound reproduces the local estimates used in that proof.
Its tuned-stage argument \eqref{eq:tuned-stage} therefore gives,
for a stage of $T$ accepted steps starting in this set,
\[
 \Delta_{\mathrm{end}}\le F_{\mathrm{loc}}\exp(-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}} T)
                         \Delta_{\mathrm{start}},\qquad
 F_{\mathrm{loc}}=2(36\kappa_\star)^3,
 \quad\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}=\frac{\log2}{29\sqrt{\kappa_\star}},
\]
Here $\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the objective
gaps at the stage endpoints; $F_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and
$\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$ are explicit versions of the stage constants
in \eqref{eq:tuned-stage}. The global bound gives
$f(x^K)-f_\star\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $K\ge K_{\mathrm{entry}}$.
The phase of budget $T_{\mathrm{adapt}}$ starts at
$2(T_{\mathrm{adapt}}-1)\ge K_{\mathrm{entry}}$ and hence lies in this sublevel.
For every subsequent tuned stage, its budget $T$ satisfies
$T\ge T_{\mathrm{adapt}}\ge2\log F_{\mathrm{loc}}/\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
Its contraction is therefore at most
$\exp(-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}} T/2)$.

In a phase with budget $T_j\ge T_{\mathrm{adapt}}$, the completed tuned
stages since the phase of budget $T_{\mathrm{adapt}}$ have total budget
$T_j-T_{\mathrm{adapt}}$. The intervening steps are monotone, so every
iterate in this phase satisfies
\[
 f(x^K)-f_\star\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}
       \exp[-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(T_j-T_{\mathrm{adapt}})/2].
\]
This also holds in the first such phase, by monotonicity.
Since $K<4T_j$, it implies \eqref{eq:controlled-finite-tail}.
Solving that inequality for $K$ proves
\eqref{eq:controlled-finite-complexity}. Finally, the next power
of two is less than twice its positive threshold,
$\log F_{\mathrm{loc}}=O(\log(2+\kappa_\star))$, and
$\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}^{-1}=O(\sqrt{\kappa_\star})$.
These facts prove \eqref{eq:controlled-separated-costs}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The original three-direction space is contained in
$\widehat{\mathcal S}^k$. The current gradient belongs to this enlarged
space, and $y^{k+1}-y^0=(y^k-y^0)+s^k\in\widehat{\mathcal S}^k$.

label: prop:inexact-model
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:inexact-model}
Retain the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} for the fixed
version and Theorem~\ref{thm:ag-rate} for the adaptive version.
For the nondegenerate local claims, retain the assumptions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:local} and bounded model coefficients.
At a nonstationary iterate, replace the exact model minimizer by any
$s^k\in\mathcal S^k$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inexact-model}
 \left\|\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\left(
 \nabla f(x^k)+\nabla^2 f(x^k)s^k
       +H_k\|s^k\|s^k\right)\right\|
 \le\frac{H_k}{6}\|s^k\|^2,\qquad H_k>0.
\end{equation}
Here $H_k=H$ for the fixed algorithm, while in backtracking $H_k$
denotes the coefficient of the current trial. The projection
$\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}$ is Euclidean.
Keep the same search spaces, aggregate update, and, in the adaptive
case, the same two Taylor acceptance tests
\eqref{eq:ftest}--\eqref{eq:gtest}.
Then monotonicity, bounded backtracking parameters, and the global
$O(\sqrt{1+\log(K+1)}/(K+1)^2)$ rate continue to hold, with changed
universal constants. With the deterministic epochs of
Section~\ref{sec:restarted-rate}, the global rate is $O(K^{-2})$,
again with changed constants.
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:local}, the local projection decomposition
and the local linear guarantee of Theorem~\ref{thm:local} also remain
valid, including across restarts.
The local PL conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:local-pl} hold under
its accumulation-point assumption. For adaptive coefficients,
additionally suppose $H_k\ge H_{\min}>0$ for all sufficiently
large $k$, where $H_{\min}$ is not supplied to the algorithm.
The contraction factor is
\[
 q=1-\frac{2\mu}{7(L_0+\sqrt{(12/5)HL_0D_0})}.
\]
Decrease $\mu$ if needed to ensure $0<q<1$. In the finite-length
and iterate-error bounds, replace $(2H/3)^{1/3}$ by $(H/2)^{1/3}$
for fixed coefficients, or by $(H_{\min}/2)^{1/3}$ for adaptive
coefficients under the stated lower-bound condition.

For each trial, any algebraic solver whose iterates converge to the
reduced-model minimizer eventually meets \eqref{eq:inexact-model}.
Checking and refining this
criterion uses the cached reduced Hessian and gradient, and requires
no additional function, gradient, or Hessian-vector oracle calls.
For a specified geometric bisection solver,
Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic-inner-work} gives an explicit bound on the
number of reduced linear solves. Projections and the reduced coefficients
remain exact.

label: lem:cacu-budgets
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cacu-budgets}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian}, let $s^k$ be
an accepted step of Algorithm~\ref{alg:cacusesop} with an exact
subspace fallback. Put $d_k=f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})$.
Backtracking terminates, and
\begin{align}
 d_k&\ge\tfrac12(s^k)^T\nabla^2f(x^k)s^k
                     +\tfrac{2H_k}{3}\|s^k\|^3,
 \label{eq:cacu-cubic-decrease}\\
 \|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2
 &\le3\bigl(L_0+\sqrt{4HL_0D_0}\bigr)d_k,
 \label{eq:cacu-gradient-budget}\\
 \|e^{k+1}\|
 &\le\left(\tfrac{243}{2}H\right)^{1/3}d_k^{2/3}.
 \label{eq:cacu-defect-budget}
\end{align}
Here $d_k$ is the accepted decrease, and
$e^{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal V^{k+1}}\nabla f(x^{k+1})$ is the gradient
component removed before updating the aggregate.
At most $r_k\le5$ HVPs are used in total over all trials of the step.
If the accepted line candidate passes the residual test, the total is one.
head: environment
name: One-step bounds for CaCuSESOP

title: Proof
body_md:
Both candidates minimize the cubic model over a space containing the
gradient: its line or $\mathcal S^k$. Both therefore satisfy
\[
 \nabla f(x^k)^Ts^k+
 (s^k)^T\nabla^2f(x^k)s^k+H_k\|s^k\|^3=0.
\]
The first-exit argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance} applies to the
line candidate at every trial coefficient at least $H$, so the first
backtracking loop terminates. If the residual test fails, the full
model step starts at the coefficient accepted by that loop. The same
first-exit argument applies to this candidate at every coefficient at
least $H$, so the second loop also terminates. Both loops use the same
dyadic grid. As in Proposition~\ref{prop:counts}, the first tested
coefficient on that grid that is at least $H$ is smaller than $2H$;
hence the final accepted coefficient satisfies $H_k\le2H$.
At an accepted step, the displayed identity and the function
certificate give \eqref{eq:cacu-cubic-decrease}.
Both candidates have model value no greater than that at any negative
gradient step. The comparison in
Lemma~\ref{lem:gradient-decrease} therefore gives
\eqref{eq:cacu-gradient-budget}.

For the line candidate, \eqref{eq:cacu-trial-residual} bounds the
projected model residual by $H_k\|s^k\|^2$; for an exact fallback this
residual is zero. Adding the gradient Taylor remainder and the model
regularization gradient gives
\[
 \|\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\nabla f(x^{k+1})\|
 \le3H_k\|s^k\|^2.
\]
Since $\mathcal V^{k+1}\subseteq\mathcal S^k$, the cubic decrease gives
\[
 \|e^{k+1}\|\le
 3H_k\left(\frac{3d_k}{2H_k}\right)^{2/3}.
\]
Cubing its coefficient yields
$27H_k^3(3/(2H_k))^2=243H_k/4$, proving
\eqref{eq:cacu-defect-budget}.
The first HVP is reused if the remaining $r_k-1$ products are formed;
all products are retained across backtracking trials. Consequently the
line branch uses one HVP and the fallback branch uses at most $r_k\le5$
in total. At the transition to the fallback, the already accepted line
candidate causes at most one extra pair of function and gradient
evaluations, but no extra HVP.

title: Proof
body_md:
The epoch potential uses only the gradient and correction-error bounds,
the weight recurrence, and correction-space containment.
With the constants of Lemma~\ref{lem:cacu-budgets}, its completed-epoch
error term is bounded by
\[
 \frac{512}{27}\,\frac{243}{2}HD^3
 =2304HD^3,
\]
where $D$ is the radius of the current sublevel about $x^\star$.
The deterministic-epoch induction and the global stage of the
controller thus give the first displayed rate, since $64\cdot81=5184$.

On a current sublevel, let $L$ bound the Hessian norm and $D$
bound the distance to $x^\star$. If its Hessian also satisfies
$\nabla^2 f\succeq\mu I$, write
$C_{\mathrm{grad}}=3(L+\sqrt{4HLD})$ for the gradient-decrease
constant. The epoch curvature term $\Gamma$ and first-step gap fraction
$\theta$ from the controller proof become
\[
 \Gamma=\frac{C_{\mathrm{grad}}}{\mu}+\frac{4608HD}{\mu},
 \qquad \theta=\frac{2\mu}{C_{\mathrm{grad}}}.
\]
In the transition region of
Corollary~\ref{cor:explicit-transition},
$D\le \mu_\star/(4096H)$,
$\mu=(1023/1024)\mu_\star$, and
$L\le(1025/1024)L_\star$.
Hence $C_{\mathrm{grad}}<8L_\star$ and
\[
 \Gamma<\frac{1024}{1023}
             \left(8\kappa_\star+\frac98\right)
       <10\kappa_\star<19\kappa_\star,
 \qquad \theta>\frac{1}{9\kappa_\star}.
\]
The bounds on completed epochs and adaptation therefore retain the
local exponent and finite-transition constants. The entry estimate
uses the new global constant.

For finite fallbacks, Appendix~\ref{app:finite-solves} gives
$C_{\mathrm{grad}}=7(L+\sqrt{(12/5)HLD})$ and a defect coefficient whose
cube is $(2197/27)H$. These also cover the gradient bound of the
line branch, and $2197/54<243/4$. Use the larger defect coefficient
of the line branch for both. The same epoch term $2304HD^3$ and
the second displayed rate follow. The transition-region bound
$C_{\mathrm{grad}}<8L_\star$ was proved in that appendix, so the same local
argument applies. No extra objective-oracle call is needed to enforce
the finite fallback criterion.

title: Theorem~\ref{thm:oracle-lower-bound} (restated)
body_md:
A vector-oracle call returns either $\nabla f(x)$ or
$\nabla^2f(x)v$. Consider algorithms starting at $0$ for which every
query point, HVP input vector, and output point belongs to the linear
span of previously returned vectors; before the first call this span
is $\{0\}$. Scalar coefficients may depend arbitrarily on the observed
information. Memory, scalar computations, and function-value queries
within the available span are unrestricted. Every gradient or HVP
evaluation counts, including the initial gradient and any inner calls.

For every integer call budget $M\ge1$, there exists a convex nonquadratic
$C^\infty$ function $f:\mathbb R^{M+2}\to\mathbb R$ with compact sublevel sets
and a unique minimizer $x^\star$, such that
\[
 0\preceq\nabla^2f(x)\preceq3I\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^{M+2}).
\]
Its smallest global Hessian Lipschitz constant is exactly $2$,
so $H=1$ is a valid supplied bound. Its third derivative is globally
$32$-Lipschitz in the induced multilinear norm. For
$\mathcal C_0=\{x:f(x)\le f(0)\}$, the level-set constants are
\[
 L_0=\max_{x\in\mathcal C_0}\|\nabla^2f(x)\|=1,
 \qquad D_0=\max_{x\in\mathcal C_0}\|x-x^\star\|=1.
\]
On this single function, every algorithm in the stated class and
every output $x$ obtained after at most $M$ vector-oracle calls satisfy
\[
 f(x)-f_\star\ge\frac{1}{2\cosh^2(2)(M+1)^2},
 \qquad f_\star=f(x^\star).
\]
Monotonicity is not required. In particular, a uniformly bounded
number of gradient and HVP calls per outer iteration cannot yield
a uniform dimension-independent $O(k^{-3})$ guarantee with constants
depending only on the displayed smoothness and level-set bounds.

{Step 1: choose the spectrum and the quadratic minimizer.}
Put $\mu=(M+1)^{-2}$. Choose $M+1$ distinct

\[
 \lambda_i=\frac{1+\mu}{2}

 \qquad i=0,\ldots,M.

They decrease from $\lambda_0=1$ to $\lambda_M=\mu$. Define

\[
 \ell_i(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le j\le M\\j\ne i}}
             \frac{t-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j},
 \qquad W_M=\sum_{i=0}^M|\ell_i(0)|,
 \qquad w_i=\frac{|\ell_i(0)|}{W_M}.

 \qquad (u^\star)_i=\sqrt{\frac{\mu w_i}{\lambda_i}},

iterate. The smallest and largest eigenvalues of $A$ are $\mu$
and $1$, respectively, and
\[
 q(u^\star)=0,\qquad q(0)=\frac\mu2.
\]

multiple of the right-hand side in Meinardus' example as described

{Step 2: bound the best point in the available polynomial space.}

\[

For every $u\in\mathcal K_M$, there is a polynomial $p$ of
degree at most $M$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lower-polynomial-error}
 u-u^\star=-p(A)u^\star,\qquad p(0)=1.
\end{equation}
Indeed, writing $u=\sum_{j=1}^M a_jA^ju^\star$ gives

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 1&=\left(\sum_{i=0}^M\ell_i(0)p(\lambda_i)\right)^2\\
  &\le\left(\sum_{i=0}^M\frac{\ell_i(0)^2}{w_i}\right)

   =W_M^2\sum_{i=0}^M w_ip(\lambda_i)^2.
 \end{aligned}

 \end{aligned}
\]
We used $\log(1+a)\le a$ in the last step. Thus every point in
$\mathcal K_M$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lower-quadratic-bound}
 q(u)\ge\frac{1}{2\cosh^2(2)(M+1)^2}.
\end{equation}
This bound concerns the entire space, regardless of how a point
inside it is selected.

{Step 3: make the objective nonquadratic with fixed constants.}
A quadratic has constant Hessian. To obtain a genuinely nonquadratic
example whose smallest global Hessian Lipschitz constant is exactly
two, define
\[
 \eta(t)=
 \begin{cases}
  \exp\!\left(4-\dfrac1{t(1-t)}\right),&0<t<1,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \phi(t)=\int_0^t(t-v)^2\eta(v)\,dv.
\]
The function $\eta$ is smooth, with every derivative vanishing at
$0$ and $1$. It satisfies $0\le\eta\le1$ and $\eta(1/2)=1$.
Differentiating the integral gives
\[
 \phi''(t)=2\int_0^t\eta(v)\,dv,\qquad
 \phi'''(t)=2\eta(t),\qquad
 0\le\phi''(t)<2.
\]
In particular, $\phi$ is smooth, convex, and nonnegative, and it and
all its derivatives vanish on $(-\infty,0]$. For $0<t<1$, set
$a=t(1-t)$. Then
\[
 |\eta'(t)|\le e^{4-1/a}a^{-2}\le16.
\]
For the second inequality, put $y=1/a\ge4$ and use that
$e^{4-y}y^2$ decreases on $[4,\infty)$ and equals $16$ at $4$.
Outside $[0,1]$ the derivative vanishes. Hence
$\max|\phi'''|=2$ and $|\phi''''|\le32$.

Append one scalar coordinate $t$ to $u\in\mathbb R^{M+1}$ and define
\[
 f(u,t)=q(u)+\frac12t^2+\phi(t-2).
\]
This function is convex, smooth, nonquadratic, and coercive. Its
unique minimizer is $x^\star=(u^\star,0)$, with $f_\star=0$.
Its Hessian is the block diagonal matrix
\[
 \nabla^2f(u,t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 A&0\\0&1+\phi''(t-2)
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
so $0\preceq\nabla^2f\preceq3I$. Its only varying Hessian entry
has derivative $\phi'''(t-2)$. Thus the global Hessian Lipschitz
constant is at most two, and it cannot be smaller because
$\phi'''(1/2)=2$. The only nonzero component of the third derivative
is $\phi'''(t-2)$ in the added coordinate. Its derivative is bounded
by $32$, proving the stated Lipschitz bound in the induced multilinear
norm. All these constants are independent of $M$.

Since $f(0,0)=\mu/2$ and $\phi\ge0$, a point in the initial
sublevel must satisfy $|t|\le\sqrt\mu\le1/2$. At every such point
$\phi(t-2)=0$. It follows in both directions that
\[
 \mathcal C_0
 =\{(u,t):(u-u^\star)^TA(u-u^\star)+t^2\le\mu\}.
\]
The Hessian is constant on this ellipsoid, with largest eigenvalue
one, so $L_0=1$. The smallest eigenvalue of its defining matrix is
$\mu$, which gives radius one about $(u^\star,0)$. That radius is
attained along an eigenvector of $A$ for $\mu$, so $D_0=1$.

\bf} 
{Step 4: count information, including momentum and inner calls.}
We now prove by induction that, after $j$ vector-oracle calls, every
returned vector lies in $\mathcal K_j\times\{0\}$. Before the first
call the available space is $\{0\}$. Suppose the claim holds after
$j$ calls. Every permitted query point then has the form $(u,0)$
with $u\in\mathcal K_j$, and every permitted HVP input has the
form $(v,0)$ with $v\in\mathcal K_j$. On this entire subspace,
\[
 \nabla f(u,0)=(Au-Au^\star,0),\qquad
 \nabla^2f(u,0)(v,0)=(Av,0).
\]
Each returned vector belongs to $\mathcal K_{j+1}\times\{0\}$.
The earlier vectors remain there as well, since the spaces are
nested. Arbitrary scalar-dependent combinations, exact minimization
inside the available span, and function-value queries cannot enlarge
that span. This proves the induction.

In particular, after at most $M$ vector-oracle calls every output
has the form $(u,0)$ with $u\in\mathcal K_M$. Since
$f(u,0)=q(u)$, inequality~\eqref{eq:lower-quadratic-bound} proves
the claimed lower bound for every such output. The construction
depends only on $M$, not on the algorithm.
The added coordinate remains zero even when query points leave
$\mathcal C_0$, so neither monotonicity nor containment of the queries
in the initial sublevel was used.

To spell out the role of momentum, an extrapolate
$y^k=x^k+\beta_k(x^k-x^{k-1})$ remains in the span containing
the two iterates, for every adaptively chosen scalar $\beta_k$.
Evaluating a gradient or an HVP there is already one of the calls
covered by the induction. Retaining all earlier vectors or solving
the restricted model more accurately does not change this argument.

Finally, suppose an algorithm uses at most $b+ck$ vector-oracle
calls through outer iteration $k$, with fixed nonnegative constants
$b,c$. Apply the construction with
$M=\max\{1,\lceil b+ck\rceil\}$. The resulting worst-case gap is
at least a constant multiple of $(k+1)^{-2}$, with the constant
depending only on $b,c$.
This contradicts a uniform bound $C/(k+1)^3$ whose constant and
starting index are independent of dimension and depend only on the
fixed displayed problem bounds. The same comparison rules out any
uniform $o(k^{-2})$ bound in this oracle model.
It concerns a family of problems of increasing dimension, so it
does not preclude faster local convergence on a fixed problem.

label: thm:global-bt
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Finite backtracking and bounded coefficients

title: Proof
body_md:
Each trial coefficient is positive, so its cubic model has a unique
minimizer. Any trial with $\widehat H\ge H$ passes both certificates:
Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance} first places its segment in $\mathcal C_0$,
and the two Taylor estimates then apply there. Doubling therefore
terminates. At an accepted step, model minimality and the function
certificate give $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)$.

If the first trial passes, $H_k=H_{k-1}/2$.
Otherwise the preceding rejected coefficient was less than $H$,
so $H_k<2H$. Induction proves \eqref{eq:global-Mbound}.
Rejected trials below $H$ may leave $\mathcal C_0$; no estimate
outside that set is used.
head: environment

label: thm:ag-rate
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ag-rate}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian},
Algorithm~\ref{alg:adaptive-cubic} without restarts satisfies
\[
 f(x^K)-f_\star\le C(L_0D_0^2+H_{\max}D_0^3)
       \frac{\sqrt{1+\log(K+1)}}{(K+1)^2}\qquad(K\ge0)
\]
for a universal constant $C$, with $H_{\max}$ from
\eqref{eq:global-Mbound}. No positive lower bound on $H_k$ is required.
head: environment
name: Global rate with adaptive regularization

label: eq:adaptive-decrease-constant
title: Proof
body_md:
The stationary initial point is immediate. Otherwise define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adaptive-decrease-constant}
 \mathcal L=L_0+\sqrt{2H_{\max}L_0D_0}>0.
\end{equation}
Stationarity of the accepted model, followed by its function certificate,
gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adaptive-two-decreases}
 f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})
 \ge\tfrac12(s^k)^T\nabla^2f(x^k)s^k+\tfrac{2H_k}{3}\|s^k\|^3.
\end{equation}
Since $H_k\le H_{\max}$ and $\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\le L_0D_0$,
the gradient comparison in Lemma~\ref{lem:gradient-decrease}
applies to the accepted model with the present $\mathcal L$.
It gives
\[
 \|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2
 \le3\mathcal L\bigl(f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})\bigr).
\]

The projected stationarity equation and \eqref{eq:gtest} also give
$\|\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\nabla f(x^{k+1})\|\le2H_k\|s^k\|^2$.
Since the correction space is contained in $\mathcal S^k$,
\begin{align*}
 \|e^{k+1}\|
 &\le2H_k\|s^k\|^2\\
 &\le(18H_k)^{1/3}\bigl(f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})\bigr)^{2/3}\\
 &\le(18H_{\max})^{1/3}
                   \bigl(f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})\bigr)^{2/3}.
\end{align*}
The second inequality uses \eqref{eq:adaptive-two-decreases} with
the actual $H_k>0$ and requires no uniform positive lower bound.

The gradient and correction estimates are precisely
\eqref{eq:algorithm-gradient}--\eqref{eq:defect-budget} with $H$ replaced by $H_{\max}$ and $\mathcal L$
set to \eqref{eq:adaptive-decrease-constant}.
The weights and all aggregate orthogonalities are unchanged.
Consequently, the interval sums, prefix estimates, and weight-window
argument of Section~\ref{sec:global} apply with these replacements.
Using
$\mathcal L D_0^2\le\tfrac32L_0D_0^2+H_{\max}D_0^3$
in \eqref{eq:explicit-rate} proves the stated bound. Constant
extension covers finite termination.

label: prop:adaptive-local
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:adaptive-local}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian} and
\ref{ass:local}, the adaptive method converges to $x^\star$ and
satisfies all conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:local}. This holds for

head: environment
name: Automatic local convergence with adaptation

title: Proof
body_md:
The gradient decrease bound gives
$\sum_{k=0}^\infty\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2<\infty$.
All accumulation points therefore minimize $f$. The minimizer is
unique by Lemma~\ref{lem:local-entry}; compactness gives
$x^k\to x^\star$, regardless of changes to the epoch's starting point.

For large $k$, the local Hessian lower bound and model stationarity
give $\|s^k\|\le2\|\nabla f(x^k)\|/\mu_\star$.
In Lemma~\ref{lem:local-projection}, write $u^k=x^k-x^\star$
and replace its remainder by
\[
 r^k=\nabla^2f(x^\star)u^k-\nabla f(x^k)
       +[\nabla^2f(x^\star)-\nabla^2f(x^k)]s^k-H_k\|s^k\|s^k.
\]
Because $H_k\le H_{\max}$, its norm is still
$O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2)$. The same projection decomposition
and gradient comparison in Theorem~\ref{thm:local} consequently
prove its error recurrence. The objective-gap factor follows from
the same Taylor expansion at $x^\star$.

label: cor:adaptive-pl
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:adaptive-pl}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:convex}--\ref{ass:hessian}, use the adaptive
algorithm. Suppose there exists $H_{\min}>0$ such that
$H_k\ge H_{\min}$ for all sufficiently large $k$.
If an accumulation point $\bar x$ satisfies the local PL condition
\eqref{eq:local-pl-condition}, all conclusions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-pl} hold with
\[
 q=1-\frac{2\mu}{3(L_0+\sqrt{2H_{\max}L_0D_0})}
\]
and with $(2H_{\min}/3)^{1/3}$ replacing $(2H/3)^{1/3}$ in the
finite-length and iterate-error bounds. Decrease $\mu$ if necessary
to ensure $0<q<1$. Thus the iterates eventually remain in the PL
neighborhood and converge R-linearly to $\bar x$, the gaps converge
Q-linearly, and the trajectory has finite length.
Restarts are permitted. Neither $H_{\min}$ nor the PL constant is
supplied to the algorithm. Finite termination is the immediate
alternative.
head: environment
name: Local PL convergence and finite trajectory length with backtracking

title: Proof
body_md:
The gradient-decrease estimate in Theorem~\ref{thm:ag-rate} and
\eqref{eq:adaptive-two-decreases} give, for all sufficiently large $k$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})
 &\ge\frac{\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2}
                {3(L_0+\sqrt{2H_{\max}L_0D_0})},\\
 f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})
 &\ge\frac{2H_{\min}}3\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^3.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Apply the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:local-pl} to this tail, with
$C_{\mathrm{grad}}=3(L_0+\sqrt{2H_{\max}L_0D_0})$ and
$c_{\mathrm{step}}=2H_{\min}/3>0$. Its neighborhood-invariance,
finite-length, and iterate-convergence arguments use only these
two bounds. The finitely many earlier steps add a finite amount
to the trajectory length. Gradient inclusion and the acceptance
tests are preserved across restarts.
head: environment

label: prop:counts
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:counts}
Suppose $K\ge1$ iterations have been accepted and their coefficients
satisfy the bound $H_{\max}$ in \eqref{eq:global-Mbound}.
Then the total number of trials satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trial-count}
 \sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(b_k+1)
 \le 2K+O(1).
\end{equation}
The additive constant is independent of $K$ and accounts for the
initial coefficient.
With cached values at accepted points, there is at most one function
and one gradient evaluation per trial, in addition to one initial
evaluation of each. The stated method uses at most $3K$ HVPs.
These bounds also hold across epochs that retain the accepted coefficient.
head: environment
name: Amortized trial and oracle counts

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $k\ge0$,
\[
 H_k=2^{b_k-1}H_{k-1}.
\]
Taking logarithms and summing telescopes the coefficient updates.
The bound $H_{K-1}\le2H$ gives $\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}b_k\le K+O(1)$,
with a constant independent of $K$, which proves \eqref{eq:trial-count}.
The stated evaluation order uses
a trial gradient only if the function certificate passes. The accepted
gradient is retained for the next step and the aggregate update.
All reduced solves and products $\nabla^2f(x^k)s$ use the same
cached model columns, giving at most three HVPs per accepted step.
Retaining the coefficient at epoch boundaries preserves the telescoping
inequality and changes none of these counts.

label: eq:inexact-decrease
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix one trial and write $x=x^k$, $s=s^k$, and $\widehat H=H_k$.
The trial model is
\[
 m_x(v)=\nabla f(x)^Tv+\tfrac12v^T\nabla^2f(x)v
                       +\tfrac{\widehat H}{3}\|v\|^3.
\]
For this proof, let $r$ denote the projected model gradient on the
left side of \eqref{eq:inexact-model}, before taking its norm, and put
$b=s^T\nabla^2 f(x)s\ge0$. Taking its inner product with $s$ gives
\[
 \nabla f(x)^Ts
 =-b-\widehat H\|s\|^3+r^Ts
 \le-b-\tfrac56\widehat H\|s\|^3.
\]
Since the current gradient belongs to the space and is nonzero,
$s=0$ cannot satisfy the criterion. Along the segment, the trial
cubic model therefore obeys, for $0<t\le1$,
\[
 m_x(ts)\le-t(1-t/2)b
       -\widehat Ht(5/6-t^2/3)\|s\|^3<0.
\]
When $\widehat H$ is at least the true localized half-Lipschitz
constant, the first-exit argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance}
applies to this strict inequality. The segment stays in the initial
sublevel set, and both Taylor certificates hold. At an accepted trial,
the function certificate gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inexact-decrease}
 f(x)-f(x+s)\ge-m_x(s)
 \ge\tfrac12b+\tfrac12\widehat H\|s\|^3.
\end{equation}
Thus the same backtracking thresholds and parameter bounds apply,
and accepted trials remain monotone even below the true constant.

The gradient Taylor certificate and \eqref{eq:inexact-model} imply
\begin{align*}
 \|\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\nabla f(x+s)\|
 &\le\tfrac{13}{6}\widehat H\|s\|^2\\
 &\le\tfrac{13}{6}\,2^{2/3}\widehat H^{1/3}
              (f(x)-f(x+s))^{2/3}.
\end{align*}
The fixed-coefficient version uses the corresponding Taylor bound.
For the gradient decrease bound, positive semidefiniteness and
$\nabla^2 f(x)\preceq L_0I$ give
\[
 \|\nabla f(x)\|^2
 \le3L_0 b+\tfrac{37}{12}\widehat H^2\|s\|^4.
\]
Indeed, the projected stationarity equation expresses the gradient
as the sum of $-\Pi_{\mathcal S^k}\nabla^2 f(x)s$,
$-\widehat H\|s\|s$, and $r$; the square of its norm is at most
three times the sum of their squared norms.
The same inner-product identity also gives
\[
 \widehat H\|s\|
 \le\sqrt{\tfrac65\widehat H\|\nabla f(x)\|}
 \le\sqrt{\tfrac65\widehat H L_0D_0}.
\]
Combining these estimates with \eqref{eq:inexact-decrease} yields
\[
 \|\nabla f(x)\|^2
 \le7\left(L_0+\sqrt{\tfrac65\widehat H L_0D_0}\right)
              (f(x)-f(x+s)).
\]
The proofs of Lemmas~\ref{lem:reserve}--\ref{lem:window} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} use only these gradient and correction-error bounds.
Substituting the displayed constants gives the same global order;
in the adaptive case use the upper bound on $H_k$.
The same two bounds also give \eqref{eq:epoch-bound} with changed
constants. Increasing the constant in the epoch induction accordingly
preserves the inverse-square rate.

Locally, $\nabla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I$ for some $\mu>0$, and the inner-product identity
gives $\|s\|\le\|\nabla f(x)\|/\mu=O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star)$.
For bounded $H_k$, both the model regularization gradient and $r$
are $O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2)$. The local projected Newton decomposition thus retains
an $O(\|x^k-x^\star\|_\star^2)$ remainder in the search space. The proofs of Lemma~\ref{lem:local-projection} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:local} therefore apply unchanged. The displayed
decrease bounds also give the stated PL factor. The step-length
coefficient is $H/2>0$ for fixed coefficients, or $H_{\min}/2>0$
for the adaptive tail under the lower-bound condition in
Proposition~\ref{prop:inexact-model}. Apply the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-pl} to obtain neighborhood invariance,
finite trajectory length, and iterate convergence with the stated
constants, also across restarts.

Finally, for a nonzero current gradient the reduced cubic model is
coercive and strictly convex, with a unique nonzero minimizer.
Along any inner sequence converging to that minimizer, the residual
tends to zero, whereas the right side of \eqref{eq:inexact-model}
tends to a positive number. The criterion is therefore met after
finitely many inner iterations. Its evaluation needs only reduced
matrix-vector arithmetic after the original at most three HVPs
(four with the optional memory direction).

title: Proof
body_md:
For the global induction, abbreviate
\[
 C_{\mathrm{inexact}}=81D_0^2
 \left[\tfrac72\left(L_0+\sqrt{\tfrac65H_{\max}L_0D_0}\right)

These estimates hold through every reset. The weighted decrease
estimate and weighted Young inequality used in
\eqref{eq:epoch-bound} therefore give, for a completed epoch
of $4t+1$ steps,
\[
 9t^2\Delta_{\mathrm{end}}
 \le (t^2-t)\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}
       +\frac{C_{\mathrm{grad}}}2D^2
       +\frac{512}{27}C_{\mathrm{corr}}^3D^3
 \le (t^2-t)\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}
       +\frac{C_{\mathrm{grad}}}2D^2+1024H_{\max}D^3.
\]
Here $\Delta_{\mathrm{start}},\Delta_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the objective gaps
at the epoch endpoints, and
$(512/27)(2197/54)=562432/729<1024$.
The deterministic-epoch induction now gives the base bound
$C_{\mathrm{inexact}}/(K+1)^2$. The global-stage argument in
Theorem~\ref{thm:automatic-acceleration} gives the stated factor
$64$ for the controller.

On a sublevel where $\nabla^2 f\succeq\mu I$, the same epoch
estimate yields
\[
 \Delta_{\mathrm{end}}\le
 \frac{t^2-t+\Gamma}{9t^2}\Delta_{\mathrm{start}},\qquad
 \Gamma=\frac{C_{\mathrm{grad}}}{\mu}+\frac{2048H_{\max}D}{\mu}.
\]
The first step also ensures an epoch decrease of at least
$\theta\Delta_{\mathrm{start}}$, where $\theta=2\mu/C_{\mathrm{grad}}$.
Thus the controller proof uses the same two estimates,
with these new analysis constants. Their proofs need only gradient
inclusion and correction-space containment, so they apply to the
three-direction variant as well.

The explicit transition constants can also be retained. Write
$\mu_\star=\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x^\star))$ and
$L_\star=\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2f(x^\star))$.
In the transition region constructed in
Corollary~\ref{cor:explicit-transition}, the radius bound
$\rho=\mu_\star/(2048H_{\max})$ and the Hessian Lipschitz bound give
\[
 \mu=\frac{1023}{1024}\mu_\star,\qquad
 L\le\frac{1025}{1024}L_\star,\qquad D\le\rho.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \sqrt{\frac65H_{\max}LD}\le\frac{L_\star}{32},\qquad
 C_{\mathrm{grad}}<8L_\star,
\]
and hence
\[
 \Gamma\le\frac{1024}{1023}(8\kappa_\star+1)
           <10\kappa_\star<19\kappa_\star,\qquad
 \theta\ge\frac{1023}{4096\kappa_\star}
      >\frac1{9\kappa_\star}.
\]
The geometric localization using
$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mu_\star^3/(2^{25}H_{\max}^2)$ depends only on
monotonicity and the Hessian Lipschitz bound, so it is unaffected
by the model residual. The bounds on the tuner length, completed-stage
progress, and phase accumulation therefore apply with the same
root exponent and finite-tail constants.
Only the global constant used to bound entry changes.

Finally, all residual checks use the cached reduced model.
The finite-termination and oracle arguments of
Proposition~\ref{prop:inexact-model} apply to every trial.
A stationary initial point, or subsequent finite termination,
is covered by constant extension.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cubic-inner-work}
For a nonstationary trial, retain the notation $Q^k,B^k,\widehat H$
of this appendix. Choose a computable $L\ge\|B^k\|$, for example
$L=\operatorname{tr}B^k$, and define
\[
 a(\lambda)=-(B^k+\lambda I)^{-1}(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k),\qquad
 \psi(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{\widehat H\|a(\lambda)\|},
 \qquad \lambda>0.
\]
The unique root of $\psi(\lambda)=1$ lies in $[\ell,U]$, where
\[
 U=\sqrt{\widehat H\|\nabla f(x^k)\|},\qquad
 \ell=\frac{U^2}{L+U}.
\]
Let $J_{\mathrm{inner}}$ denote the number of inner bisections,
which is separate from the accepted-step count $K$. If $L>0$, set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic-inner-count}
 J_{\mathrm{inner}}=\max\left\{0,\left\lceil
 \log_2\!\left(\frac{2\log(1+L/U)}{\log(7/6)}\right)
 \right\rceil\right\}.
\end{equation}
Starting with $[\ell,U]$, perform $J_{\mathrm{inner}}$ geometric bisections: evaluate
$\psi$ at the geometric mean of the endpoints, replace the lower
endpoint when this value is at most one, and otherwise replace the
upper endpoint. Let $v$ be the final upper endpoint. Then
$s=Q^k a(v)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:inexact-model} with $H_k=\widehat H$.
The procedure uses at most $J_{\mathrm{inner}}+1$ reduced linear solves, including a
final evaluation at $v$, and no additional objective-oracle calls.
If $L=0$, the bracket collapses to $\ell=U$ and one reduced solve
gives the exact model minimizer.

name: A constructive bound for the reduced cubic solve

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the current gradient belongs to the search space,
$\|(Q^k)^T\nabla f(x^k)\|=\|\nabla f(x^k)\|>0$.
The spectral bounds $0\preceq B^k\preceq LI$ imply
\[
 \frac{\|\nabla f(x^k)\|}{L+\lambda}
 \le\|a(\lambda)\|
 \le\frac{\|\nabla f(x^k)\|}{\lambda}.
\]
The function $\psi$ is strictly increasing. The upper norm bound
gives $\psi(U)\ge1$, while the lower bound and $\ell\le U$ give
\[
 \psi(\ell)\le\frac{\ell(L+\ell)}{U^2}
              \le\frac{\ell(L+U)}{U^2}=1.
\]
For any $0<u\le v$, diagonalizing the positive semidefinite matrix
$B^k$ gives
\[
 1\le\frac{\|a(u)\|}{\|a(v)\|}\le\frac vu,
 \qquad
 \frac{\psi(v)}{\psi(u)}\le\left(\frac vu\right)^2.
\]
Every bisection preserves the root bracket and halves its logarithmic
width. If $[u,v]$ is the final interval, then
\[
 1\le\psi(v)\le(v/u)^2
 =\exp\!\left(2^{1-J_{\mathrm{inner}}}\log(U/\ell)\right)\le\frac76,
\]
where $\log(U/\ell)=\log(1+L/U)$ and
\eqref{eq:cubic-inner-count} gives the last inequality.
For $s=Q^k a(v)$, the projected model gradient is exactly
$(\widehat H\|s\|-v)s$. Therefore its norm is
\[
 (\psi(v)-1)\widehat H\|s\|^2
 \le\frac{\widehat H}{6}\|s\|^2,
\]
as required. Each midpoint and the final endpoint require at most
one reduced solve; the initial bracket needs no numerical root test.
If $L=0$, then $B^k=0$ and $U=\ell$ solves the secular equation exactly.
